speakerBio: Endocrinologist who teaches the divalent ions as one interlocking family and whose ward mantra is 'saline before the bisphosphonate, and always check the magnesium'.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 67-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of breast cancer is brought in confused, constipated and vomiting, having barely passed urine for two days. She is profoundly dehydrated. The lab phones a critical result: corrected calcium 3.6 mmol/L. This is a hypercalcaemic crisis — and the first drug is not a bisphosphonate, it is litres of saline. This session sweeps through the divalent-ion emergencies — calcium, phosphate and magnesium — because they travel together, they mimic each other, and one of them (magnesium) is the silent enabler that makes the others impossible to fix. We finish where session 11 left off: you cannot correct calcium or potassium while the magnesium is on the floor.

1 · 🧮 First, correct the calcium — the formula everyone should know

Roughly half of plasma calcium is bound to albumin; only the ionised fraction is biologically active. A hypoalbuminaemic patient has a low total calcium but may have a normal ionised calcium — so always correct before you act:

Corrected calcium = measured total calcium + 0.02 × (40 − albumin in g/L) mmol/L
(i.e. add 0.02 mmol/L for every 1 g/L that albumin is below 40).

When in doubt — or in the critically ill, acid–base disturbed, or citrate-anticoagulated patient — measure the ionised calcium directly on a blood gas, as the albumin correction is only an approximation. Acidosis raises ionised calcium (less protein binding); alkalosis lowers it (the mechanism behind tetany in hyperventilation).

💡 The calcium chart in one breath

Calcium is set by the interplay of PTH (raises Ca: bone resorption, renal reabsorption, activates vitamin D), vitamin D (raises Ca: gut absorption), and the counter-regulator calcitonin (lowers Ca modestly). Phosphate moves inversely to calcium under PTH, and magnesium is required for PTH secretion and action. Hold that quartet in mind — it explains every disorder below.

2 · ⬆️ Hypercalcaemia — mechanism and the two big causes

90% of hypercalcaemia is either malignancy or primary hyperparathyroidism. The distinction is usually made by one test — the PTH — and the clinical tempo.

FeaturePrimary hyperparathyroidismMalignancy
Typical settingOutpatient, well, incidental finding, chronicInpatient, unwell, rapid, known/obvious cancer
PTHHigh or inappropriately normalSuppressed (low)
MechanismAutonomous adenoma (85%) → ↑PTHPTHrP (squamous/breast/renal); osteolytic mets; 1,25-vit D (lymphoma)
Calcium levelUsually mild (<3.0)Often severe (>3.0)
PhosphateLow (PTH is phosphaturic)Variable

The mechanisms of malignant hypercalcaemia:

  • PTHrP (humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy) — the commonest; squamous lung, breast, renal, head/neck tumours secrete PTH-related peptide, mimicking PTH but suppressing the real thing.
  • Osteolytic bone metastases / myeloma — local bone destruction and cytokine-driven osteoclast activation.
  • Ectopic 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D — lymphomas and granulomatous disease (sarcoid, TB) convert vitamin D unregulated.

"Stones, bones, groans, moans" — the clinical picture

  • Stones — renal calculi, nephrocalcinosis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria → dehydration → worsening calcium: a vicious cycle).
  • Bones — bone pain, osteitis fibrosa cystica, fractures.
  • Groans — abdominal: constipation, nausea, vomiting, peptic ulcers, pancreatitis.
  • Moans (psychic) — fatigue, depression, confusion, drowsiness, coma; ECG shows a short QT.
🎯 The dehydration vicious cycle

Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI (blocks ADH action) and anorexia/vomiting → the patient becomes profoundly volume-deplete → GFR falls → the kidney can't excrete calcium → calcium climbs further → more polyuria and vomiting. Breaking this cycle with aggressive rehydration is why saline is the first-line treatment, before any bone-targeted drug.

3 · 💊 Treating hypercalcaemia — the ordered ladder

Consistent with Endocrine Society guidance, treat severe (>3.5 or symptomatic) hypercalcaemia in this sequence:

StepTreatmentDetail / onset
1. RehydrateIV 0.9% saline — the cornerstone~3–4 L/24h (e.g. 200–300 mL/h), titrated to volume status; restores GFR and promotes calciuresis. Onset: hours.
2. AntiresorptiveIV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg, or pamidronate)Inhibits osteoclasts; the definitive lowering agent but takes 2–4 days for full effect and lasts weeks. Adjust dose in renal impairment.
3. BridgeCalcitonin (SC/IM)Works fast (within hours) to bridge the gap while the bisphosphonate takes effect, but tachyphylaxis within 48h — short-term only.
4. Refractory / renal failureDenosumab; haemodialysisDenosumab (RANKL inhibitor) for bisphosphonate-refractory or renally-impaired malignant hypercalcaemia. Dialysis for crisis with renal failure.
5. SpecificGlucocorticoidsFor granulomatous / lymphoma (vitamin-D-mediated) hypercalcaemia — reduce 1,25-vit D production. No use in PTHrP disease.
⚠️ Do NOT reach for loop diuretics as a routine treatment

Old teaching of "furosemide to promote calciuresis" is outdated and can worsen the dehydration that drives the hypercalcaemia. Loop diuretics are reserved for managing fluid overload once the patient is fully rehydrated (e.g. in heart failure), not as a primary calcium-lowering strategy. Fill the tank with saline first; only then, if overloaded, consider a loop.

💡 Definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism is surgical

For symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (or asymptomatic with calcium >0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit, age <50, reduced eGFR/renal stones, or reduced bone density), the cure is parathyroidectomy. Cinacalcet (a calcimimetic) is an option when surgery isn't feasible.

4 · ⬇️ Hypocalcaemia — causes and the neuromuscular signs

Low ionised calcium makes nerves and muscles hyperexcitable: perioral and digital paraesthesiae, cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, and ECG prolonged QT (torsades risk).

MechanismCauses
PTH deficiencyPost-thyroidectomy / post-parathyroidectomy (commonest surgical cause), autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge, neck irradiation
Vitamin D deficiencyDietary/sunlight lack, malabsorption, CKD (failed 1α-hydroxylation), liver disease
Magnesium relatedHypomagnesaemia (impairs PTH secretion & action — refractory hypocalcaemia)
Sequestration / chelationHungry bone syndrome (post-parathyroidectomy), acute pancreatitis, tumour lysis, citrate (massive transfusion), rhabdomyolysis, hyperphosphataemia
OtherAlkalosis (↑protein binding → symptomatic despite normal total Ca), pseudohypoparathyroidism

The two eponymous signs

  • Chvostek's sign — tapping over the facial nerve (anterior to the ear) triggers ipsilateral facial twitching. Sensitive but not specific (positive in ~10% of normals).
  • Trousseau's sign — inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 minutes induces carpopedal spasm (flexed wrist/MCPs, extended fingers). More specific; a classic bedside demonstration of latent tetany.
🎯 Treating hypocalcaemia

Acute symptomatic (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, QT prolongation): IV calcium — 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 min, repeated or followed by an infusion, with cardiac monitoring. Chronic/mild: oral calcium + vitamin D (activated forms — alfacalcidol/calcitriol — if CKD or hypoparathyroidism). And always: check and replace magnesium, or the calcium will not correct.

5 · 🧬 Phosphate — the mirror of calcium

Phosphate largely moves inversely to calcium and is regulated by PTH and FGF-23 (both phosphaturic).

HyperphosphataemiaHypophosphataemia
CausesCKD (reduced excretion — the big one), tumour lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, hypoparathyroidism, excess vitamin D, phosphate enemasRefeeding syndrome, DKA recovery (insulin drives PO₄ into cells), alcoholism, hyperparathyroidism, respiratory alkalosis, Fanconi, poor intake/malabsorption
ConsequenceLowers calcium; metastatic calcification; in CKD drives renal osteodystrophy & vascular calcificationMuscle weakness (incl. respiratory failure, failure to wean), rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, confusion, arrhythmia; cardiac dysfunction
TreatmentDietary restriction + oral phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer) with meals; treat/anticipate tumour lysis; dialysis if severeOral (or IV if severe/symptomatic, e.g. Phosphate Polyfusor) replacement; slow, controlled refeeding with thiamine
⚠️ Refeeding syndrome — the falling phosphate that stops the diaphragm

A starved patient (anorexia, alcoholism, prolonged NBM, post-bariatric) given carbohydrate suddenly secretes insulin, which drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells — the plasma levels crash, and hypophosphataemia can cause respiratory muscle failure, arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis and death. Identify high-risk patients, start feeding slowly (e.g. 10 kcal/kg/day), give thiamine and B-vitamins before feeding, and replace phosphate/potassium/magnesium aggressively with daily monitoring.

6 · 🧲 Magnesium — the great enabler

Magnesium is the cation that controls the other cations. It is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes, stabilises cardiac membranes, and is required for both PTH secretion and PTH action and for the ROMK potassium channel's regulation.

HypomagnesaemiaHypermagnesaemia
CausesAlcoholism, diuretics (loop/thiazide), PPIs, diarrhoea/malabsorption, refeeding, drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors), DKARenal failure + magnesium load (antacids/laxatives), obstetric (IV magnesium for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), tumour lysis, Addison's
FeaturesRefractory hypokalaemia & hypocalcaemia, tremor, tetany, seizures, arrhythmia — prolonged QT, torsades de pointesProgressive: nausea, flushing → loss of deep tendon reflexes (~>4 mmol/L) → respiratory depression → hypotension, bradycardia, heart block → cardiac arrest
TreatmentIV magnesium sulfate (e.g. 2 g / 8 mmol over 10–20 min if arrhythmia/tetany, else slower); replace K & Ca alongsideStop magnesium; IV calcium gluconate (antagonises cardiac effects); fluids + loop diuretic; dialysis if renal failure/severe
Magnesium is the great enabler: you cannot fix a refractory potassium or a refractory calcium until you have replaced the magnesium. In obstetrics, watch reflexes — their loss is the first sign of magnesium toxicity.
💡 The eclampsia monitoring triad

Patients on IV magnesium for eclampsia are monitored for toxicity by deep tendon reflexes (lost first), respiratory rate (<12 = danger), and urine output (magnesium is renally cleared, so oliguria → accumulation). The antidote to magnesium toxicity is IV calcium gluconate — keep it at the bedside.

7 · 🧭 Master table — the divalent ions at a glance

IonHIGH — key cause & signLOW — key cause & signEmergency drug
CalciumMalignancy/PHPT; stones, bones, groans, moans; short QTPost-thyroidectomy/vit D/low Mg; Chvostek/Trousseau; long QTHigh: saline → bisphosphonate. Low: calcium gluconate
PhosphateCKD/tumour lysis; lowers Ca, calcificationRefeeding/DKA recovery; respiratory failure, weaknessHigh: binders. Low: phosphate replacement
MagnesiumRenal failure/obstetric; areflexia → resp depressionAlcohol/diuretics/PPI; refractory K & Ca, torsadesHigh: calcium gluconate. Low: magnesium sulfate
☠️ M&M — the hypercalcaemic crisis treated back-to-front

A 71-year-old man with metastatic squamous lung cancer arrived drowsy, constipated and anuric with a corrected calcium of 4.1 and an AKI (creatinine 280). The on-call team, focused on the number, gave IV zoledronic acid immediately and little else. Two problems followed. First, the calcium barely moved for three days — because a bisphosphonate takes 2–4 days to work and does nothing for the acute crisis; what he desperately needed was aggressive saline rehydration to restore his GFR and drive calciuresis, which had been neglected while he stayed volume-deplete. Second, full-dose zoledronic acid in the setting of significant renal impairment risked worsening the AKI. He deteriorated into a hypercalcaemic coma before the team escalated to vigorous saline, calcitonin as a fast-acting bridge, and denosumab for the renally-impaired refractory malignant hypercalcaemia. Lessons: (1) the first-line treatment of hypercalcaemic crisis is fluid, fluid, fluid, not the bisphosphonate; (2) a bisphosphonate is definitive but slow — bridge with calcitonin for the first 24–48h; (3) dose-adjust or choose denosumab in renal failure; (4) treat the vicious dehydration cycle before it becomes irreversible. They reached for the disease-modifying drug and forgot the resuscitation.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Always correct calcium for albumin (+0.02 per g/L below 40), or measure ionised calcium in the acid–base disturbed/critically ill.
  2. Hypercalcaemia = malignancy vs primary hyperparathyroidism in 90% — the PTH splits them (suppressed in malignancy, high/inappropriate in PHPT); remember 'stones, bones, groans, moans' and the short QT.
  3. Treat hypercalcaemic crisis in order: saline first, then IV bisphosphonate (slow), calcitonin to bridge, denosumab/dialysis if refractory or renal failure, steroids for granulomatous/lymphoma.
  4. Hypocalcaemia: post-thyroidectomy, vitamin D deficiency, low magnesium, hungry bone; Chvostek/Trousseau and long QT; IV calcium gluconate for acute tetany/seizures.
  5. Phosphate mirrors calcium: high in CKD/tumour lysis (binders); low in refeeding/DKA recovery (can cause respiratory failure — feed slowly, replace).
  6. Magnesium is the great enabler — low magnesium causes refractory hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia and torsades; high magnesium (renal failure/obstetric) causes areflexia then respiratory/cardiac arrest, reversed with IV calcium.
  7. Fix the magnesium first — it is the recurring theme of the whole electrolyte block.

moderatorQs.q: A patient presents with corrected calcium 3.7. Before any specific therapy, what is your first-line treatment and why is it, rather than a bisphosphonate, the priority?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Aggressive IV 0.9% saline rehydration — this is the cornerstone and it comes first. Severe hypercalcaemia causes a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and vomiting, leaving the patient profoundly volume-deplete; the falling GFR then prevents calcium excretion and the level spirals upward. Restoring intravascular volume with several litres of saline (e.g. 3–4 L/24h, titrated to the patient) both improves the GFR and promotes calciuresis, and it works within hours. A bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) is the definitive lowering agent but takes 2–4 days to act, so it does nothing for the acute crisis and, at full dose, can worsen an AKI. So: fill the tank first, give the bisphosphonate for durable control, and bridge the 24–48h gap with calcitonin if the patient is very symptomatic.

moderatorQs.q: How do you use the PTH and the clinical picture to separate the two commonest causes of hypercalcaemia?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Around 90% of hypercalcaemia is either primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy, and the PTH splits them. In primary hyperparathyroidism the PTH is high or inappropriately normal (it should be suppressed by a high calcium) — typically a well outpatient with mild, chronic hypercalcaemia found incidentally, often with a low phosphate. In malignancy the PTH is suppressed, and the mechanism is PTHrP (humoral hypercalcaemia — squamous, breast, renal), osteolytic metastases/myeloma, or ectopic 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma/granulomatous) — typically an unwell inpatient with rapid, severe hypercalcaemia and an obvious malignancy. So: check the PTH; if it's up it's the parathyroids, if it's down look for cancer.

moderatorQs.q: Why does hypomagnesaemia make both hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia refractory to replacement?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because magnesium sits upstream of both. For potassium: low intracellular magnesium releases the inhibition on the renal ROMK channel, so the distal nephron wastes potassium continuously — every dose you give is urinated away until the magnesium is repleted. For calcium: magnesium is required for both the secretion and the peripheral action of PTH, so hypomagnesaemia produces a functional hypoparathyroidism — PTH falls or fails to act, calcium can't be mobilised, and calcium replacement won't hold. The practical rule that unifies the whole electrolyte block is therefore: check and replace magnesium first (or alongside), or you will chase a refractory potassium and calcium all day.

audienceQs.q: My patient is 4 days post-total-thyroidectomy with tingling around the mouth and a positive Trousseau's sign. What do I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: This is post-surgical hypocalcaemia — the parathyroids have been bruised or removed, PTH has dropped, and your patient has symptomatic hypocalcaemia (perioral paraesthesiae, and a positive Trousseau's sign — carpopedal spasm on cuff inflation — is fairly specific for latent tetany). Check a corrected calcium and an ECG (looking for a prolonged QT) urgently. For symptomatic hypocalcaemia give IV calcium gluconate — 10 mL of 10% over about 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring, repeated or followed by an infusion until symptoms settle, then start oral calcium and an activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol). Also check the magnesium — low magnesium will keep the calcium down. Watch for hungry bone syndrome if there was pre-existing bone disease.

audienceQs.q: Which patients starting feeding should I worry about for refeeding syndrome, and what's the electrolyte to watch?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Worry about anyone who has been significantly undernourished or catabolic: little or no intake for >5 days, chronic alcoholism, anorexia nervosa, prolonged fasting/NBM, post-bariatric surgery, or a low BMI with recent weight loss. When you feed them carbohydrate, the insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells — and the electrolyte to watch above all is phosphate, because severe hypophosphataemia causes respiratory muscle failure, arrhythmia and death. The safe approach: start low (around 10 kcal/kg/day) and build up slowly, give thiamine and B-vitamins before and during feeding, and monitor and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily for the first several days.

audienceQs.q: A pre-eclamptic woman on IV magnesium has lost her knee reflexes. What does that mean and what do I give?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first clinical sign of magnesium toxicity — it typically appears before the more dangerous respiratory depression (respiratory rate <12) and cardiac effects (hypotension, bradycardia, heart block) that follow at higher levels. Stop the magnesium infusion immediately, check the magnesium level and renal function (magnesium is renally cleared, so any oliguria causes accumulation), and give the antidote: IV calcium gluconate (e.g. 10 mL of 10% over ~10 minutes), which antagonises magnesium's neuromuscular and cardiac effects. Support ventilation if the respiratory rate is falling. Then reassess whether magnesium can be cautiously restarted at a lower rate with closer reflex, respiratory-rate and urine-output monitoring.
